In Lesson 23 they planned and began drafting their own modern retelling of a myth. Today they finish and revise it.","enduringUnderstanding":"Writers keep the deep pattern of a myth and change the surface of the story, such as the setting, details, and point of view. This lets old stories speak to new readers and carry new messages.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 25 students return to the anchor text with Chapter 18 and analyze how the Underworld entrance is set up. They will bring the same eye for setting and detail to that reading.","performanceTask":"In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, students must explain how a retelling reinterprets a myth. Today's skill, revising a narrative and explaining what it keeps and what it changes, builds directly toward that."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"archetype","definition":"a pattern, character type, or situation that appears again and again in stories across cultures (such as the hero or the mentor)","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"retelling","definition":"a new version of an existing story, told with changes to some of its parts","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"reinterpret","definition":"to explain or present something in a new way that shows a different meaning","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"honor","definition":"to respect and keep something important (here, to keep key parts of the original story)","tier":"support"},{"word":"adverbial","definition":"a word or phrase that tells when, where, how, or why something happens","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"Ch. 18, pp. 283–top of 291 (homework)"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Quickly reconnect students to their drafts and to the big idea that a retelling can keep a pattern while changing the message.","activities":[{"id":"launch-same-pattern-new-message","title":"Same Pattern, New Message","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.9"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Take out your draft and your plan from Lesson 23. Turn to a partner and answer: What is one thing in your story that is the same as the original myth, and one thing you changed?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Yesterday you started building a modern retelling. Today you finish it and make it stronger. A good retelling is like a remix: the beat stays, but the sound is new."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What did you keep from the original myth, and what did you change?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I kept the hero pattern. My main character is an ordinary kid who gets a hard challenge and has to prove herself. But I changed the setting from ancient Greece to a middle school science fair, so the challenge is about being honest, not about fighting a monster."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Remember how Percy is a modern kid on a classic hero's quest. Riordan keeps the pattern and changes the world around it. Today you will explain your own choices the same way."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to about 3 minutes of talk. Circulate and note students who cannot name an archetypal element they kept; they may need the support table in Learning in Action."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Teach compare/classify sentence frames and a mentor model so students can explain how their retelling honors and changes the original myth.","activities":[{"id":"lab-compare-frames","title":"Comparing a Myth and a Retelling with Sentence Frames","minutes":10,"standards":["RL.6.9","W.6.4","L.6.3"],"routine":"Language Study","blocks":[{"type":"teach"  ,"text":"x"}]}]}]}
